title: Five Findings From The Forrester Wave™: Customer Experience Strategy Consulting Services, Q4 2026
summary: It’s been two years since we last evaluated CX strategy consulting services, so we were due for another peek under the hood.
body_markdown:
It’s been two years since we last evaluated CX strategy consulting services, so we were due for another peek under the hood of the vendors that are doing the most in this market (read: minimum $250 million in annual practice revenue). These firms have a wide breadth of capabilities needed to support CX strategy development, serve a global clientele, and create strategies that support experiences that are physical, digital, and a hybrid of the two.


That latter inclusion criterion has been a particularly sticky wicket in the last couple of years, as more vendors have been positioning themselves as digital experience or digital transformation partners. Since human beings still have all kinds of physical needs (and their journeys may cross digital and physical channels), this evaluation has deliberately excluded firms that primarily or solely focus on digital experience.


In the three months since this Wave kicked off, I’ve attended 24 hours of briefings, pored over hundreds of slides and questionnaire responses, and interviewed nearly three dozen reference customers. Now that[The Forrester Wave™: Customer Experience Strategy Consulting Services, Q4 2026](https://www.forrester.com/go?objectid=RES204372) has published, I can share my top five findings from this year’s Wave:


- **The great convergence is here, part one: capabilities.** Two years ago, I predicted that there would be a future convergence when the offers from business strategy consultancies, business technology consultancies, and agencies at the top echelon of this market would be similar enough that this would turn into a buyer’s market. That future has arrived: All of the firms in this evaluation have capabilities in the foundations needed to develop a CX strategy, such as CX vision development and business case development, and they also have partnerships, tools, and technology skills that enable these strategies to be brought to life. The separations between par and above or below par have narrowed considerably.
- **The great convergence is here, part two: CX philosophy (aka “practice vision”).** The practice’s vision defines the philosophy that guides the vendor’s hand when deciding what capabilities, tools, and talent it needs to support its offering. The market has largely converged on two primary themes for the practice vision, one centered on helping clients improve CX to grow their business and one to improve the ecosystem that underpins CX delivery. Both of those common visions are good and noble messages, but the broad adoption of just two themes demonstrates a lack of philosophical variety. Only two firms had truly differentiated visions by comparison to the rest of the field.
- **Everybody has and is using AI.** Earlier this year, I had an interesting conversation with a large consultancy (not in this Wave) that seemed shocked that other consultancies were using AI. I was shocked that they were shocked. If there’s anyone out there still operating under the impression that only their company understands AI, please allow me to disabuse you of that right away. Every firm in this Wave has made significant investments in AI capabilities (both human and technology), to the point where it’s clear that *AI is table stakes* . The differentiations emerge in how and where it’s being applied and how the company governs it, rather than if the firm has that expertise (which they all do).
- **Consultants are a key differentiator.** This is a harder one to use as a specific criterion, but it certainly came up enough in the reference interviews that it was worth a mention. Many customers cited either their consultancy’s team or individual consultants as the reason for their engagement’s success. Several customers emphatically stated that if it hadn’t been for a specific named person, they might have either discontinued a project or wouldn’t have even started it to begin with.
- **Clients want their consultancies to understand more than just their industry.** In my prior evaluation of the market, reference customers talked about the importance of the consultancy understanding their geography or industry — such as by having staff that speak the local language or that understand their industry’s jargon and nuances. This time, customers talked instead about the importance of consultancies understanding the context of their organization, such as how fast their own organization expects action once it makes a decision, if it operates in more of a “startup mode,” or if it has a consensus culture. The phrase “meet us where we are” came up in multiple interviews.


There are still more lessons to be learned from this year’s evaluation, so[I recommend reading the full report](https://www.forrester.com/go?objectid=RES204372) — which is now available to all Forrester clients. Use the “Compare vendors” button at the top of the report to find your best-fit vendor based on the criteria that matter most for your firm. Still have questions? I’m happy to chat on a[guidance session or inquiry](https://www.forrester.com/inquiry?bioId=BIO13627) about the results of this evaluation.
